directions: Section I, Part B: Short Answer. Time: 40 minutes. This part contains 3 short-answer questions. Answer all three questions; there is no choice. Question 1 is based on a secondary-text source (historians' interpretations). Question 2 is based on a primary-text source. Question 3 is based on a non-text source (an image). Each question has three parts (A, B, and C). Respond to all parts of each question. Use complete sentences; an outline or bulleted list alone is not acceptable.

exemplars.A: One major difference is that Roosevelt presents the war as a moral and strategic necessity driven by American duty, while Atwood presents it as a war manufactured by elites through deception. Roosevelt emphasizes Cuban suffering, American economic interests, and national honor as genuine reasons for intervention; Atwood argues that the public case for war rested on false claims, especially the blaming of Spain for the sinking of the USS Maine.
exemplars.B: The sinking of the USS Maine in Havana harbor in February 1898, which killed 266 American sailors, could support Roosevelt's interpretation. The explosion created genuine public outrage and was widely believed at the time to be Spanish sabotage, giving the McKinley administration a real crisis that made war politically unavoidable regardless of any planning behind the scenes.
exemplars.C: Senator Lodge's private message noting that an explosion in Cuba 'would settle a great many things' while an American battleship sat in Havana harbor could support Atwood's interpretation. It suggests that some expansionist leaders saw a violent incident as politically useful, which fits Atwood's claim that the war's causes were deliberately shaped rather than simply reacted to.

parts.A: Briefly explain ONE major difference between the two historians' interpretations of the United States' involvement in the Spanish-American War.
parts.B: Briefly explain how ONE historical event or development in the relevant time period could be used to support the first historian's interpretation.
parts.C: Briefly explain how ONE historical event or development in the relevant time period could be used to support the second historian's interpretation.

items.stimulus:
Source 1 — Historian A (summarized): The United States went to war with Spain in 1898 out of a mix of genuine motives: sympathy for Cubans suffering under Spanish reconcentration policies, protection of substantial American investments in Cuban sugar and tobacco, the strategic value of Cuba to a planned Central American canal, and a sense of national honor that made standing aside impossible.

Source 2 — Historian B (summarized): The Spanish-American War was brought on by deliberate deception. Yellow journalists and expansionist politicians inflamed the public with exaggerated or false stories of Spanish atrocities, and the accidental explosion of the USS Maine was falsely blamed on Spain to create the war fever that made intervention possible.

exemplars.A: One argument the document makes is that women are entitled to the same natural rights as men, including the elective franchise. By declaring that 'all men and women are created equal,' the authors claim that denying women the vote or property rights violates the same principles of equality the nation was founded on.
exemplars.B: The document deliberately mirrors the Declaration of Independence: it opens with 'We hold these truths to be self-evident,' lists grievances against men the way Jefferson listed grievances against the king, and closes by appealing to a candid world. This connection was meant to show that women's demands grew logically out of America's founding promises rather than breaking with them.
exemplars.C: One reason for limited success was that the movement's demands threatened the era's cult of domesticity, which held that respectable women belonged in the home; most Americans, including many women, rejected the call for suffrage as improper. Another reason was that the slavery crisis soon consumed national politics, pushing women's rights off the agenda until after the Civil War.

parts.A: Briefly explain ONE argument the document makes about the rights of women.
parts.B: Briefly explain how the document connects its claims to the Declaration of Independence.
parts.C: Briefly explain ONE reason the women's rights movement achieved only limited success before the Civil War.

items.stimulus: "We hold these truths to be self-evident: that all men and women are created equal; that they are endowed by their Creator with certain inalienable rights... The history of mankind is a history of repeated injuries and usurpations on the part of man toward woman, having in direct object the establishment of an absolute tyranny over her... He has never permitted her to exercise her inalienable right to the elective franchise... He has taken from her all right in property, even to the wages she earns." — Declaration of Sentiments, Seneca Falls Convention, July 1848

exemplars.A: One characteristic portrayed is the power of the urban political machine: the boss controls jobs, contracts, and favors, trading them for votes and loyalty, which made city government a system of patronage rather than public service.
exemplars.B: One reaction was civil service reform, such as the Pendleton Act of 1883, which replaced the spoils system with merit-based federal hiring and reduced the patronage the machines depended on.
exemplars.C: Another reaction was the Progressive push for structural reforms of city government itself, including the secret (Australian) ballot to weaken machine control of voting and the commission and city-manager systems designed to replace boss rule with professional administration.

parts.A: Briefly explain ONE characteristic of urban politics in the late nineteenth century as portrayed in the image.
parts.B: Briefly explain ONE reaction to, or historical change resulting from, the urban politics of the late nineteenth century.
parts.C: Briefly explain ANOTHER reaction to, or historical change resulting from, the urban politics of the late nineteenth century.

items.stimulus: Image description: Political cartoon by Frederick Burr Opper, published in Puck magazine, 1893 (public domain). A corpulent political boss, labeled as the head of the city machine, sits behind a desk handing out patronage jobs and contracts to a line of eager supporters. A ballot box sits at his feet, and ordinary voters look on from the margins while the boss's allies stuff the box. Tammany-style ward heelers hover nearby, collecting their share.
